REASONING:
**Step 1 – Project framing**  
- **Objective / PDO:** Improve access to water supply and sanitation services, integrated water‑resources management and operational performance of service providers.  
- **Scope & components:** Four components – (1) WSS in small towns & Rural Growth Centres (RGCs) + support to districts hosting refugees; (2) WSS in large towns + refugee‑district support; (3) Water‑resources management (catchment protection, groundwater study, WIS); (4) Project implementation & institutional strengthening.  
- **Delivery model:** Implemented by two IAs – Ministry of Water & Environment (MWE) and National Water & Sewerage Corporation (NWSC).  Small‑town/RGC services are managed by Umbrella Water Authorities (UWAs); large‑town services by NWSC.  A Project Support Team (PST) provides specialist support.  
- **Timeline:** Effective 14 Jun 2018; expected closing 2 Dec 2024 (≈ 6 years).  
- **Budget / financing:** Total cost US$313 m (IDA credit US$251 m, IDA grant US$29 m, KfW US$25 m, counterpart US$8 m).  
- **Key stakeholders:** GoU, MWE, NWSC, UWAs, UNHCR, Office of the Prime Minister, donors (KfW, other DPs), host‑community leaders, refugee populations, local governments.  
- **External dependencies / constraints:** Regional instability (South‑Sudan conflict), large refugee influx, climate‑change‑induced floods/droughts, donor‑fund availability, water‑resource variability, land‑acquisition processes.

**Step 2 – Category sweep (candidate risks with supporting text ≤ 25 words)**  

| ID | Description (draft) | Category | Evidence (≤25 words) |
|----|----------------------|----------|----------------------|
| R01 | Incomplete geotechnical studies may cause design changes and cost overruns. | Technical / Schedule / Financial | “Incomplete needs assessments and inadequate attention to geotechnical studies… resulting in design changes/variations during construction and consequently time and cost overruns.” |
| R02 | Minimum environmental flow (EF) may not be maintained during dry season, harming downstream users/ecosystems. | Environmental | “Namatala’s dry weather flows may not be sufficient… downstream users and aquatic biota could be affected if minimum EF is not maintained.” |
| R03 | Leakage from sewers, sludge drying beds and wastewater ponds if O&M is inadequate. | Technical | “Leakages from sewers, sludge drying beds and wastewater stabilization ponds will be minimized by regular monitoring and maintenance.” |
| R04 | Improper handling of asbestos‑cement (AC) pipes poses health/environmental hazards. | Environmental | “For AC pipes, the Environmental Management Plan includes management measures for removal, packaging, transportation and disposal of existing asbestos waste.” |
| R05 | Small‑dam safety risks if design/inspection are inadequate. | Technical / Environmental | “Qualified engineers are used to design these dams; Small Dam Guidelines will be used to ensure adherence to generic dam safety measures.” |
| R06 | Low technical expertise for solar‑powered water schemes may delay implementation. | Technical / Organizational | “The most important barrier to solar schemes is the low level of technical expertise on solar energy among WASH stakeholders.” |
| R07 | Underestimation of construction costs leads to overruns. | Financial | “Delayed construction and underestimation of the cost of works attributed to preparation of designs for works during the Project life.” |
| R08 | Revenue collection may be insufficient where tariffs do not cover costs. | Financial | “In some regions, cost recovery is not achieved. The NWSC’s financial analysis shows tariffs cover O&M but not investment costs.” |
| R09 | Debt service on the IDA loan could strain NWSC cash flow. | Financial | “Annual payments of principal and service charge would correspond to less than 1.4 % of total annual revenues after 2025.” |
| R10 | UWAs rely on donor subsidies for capital investments. | Financial / Organizational | “UWAs are still dependent on public financing for capital investments and for providing assistance on O&M related‑activities.” |
| R11 | Procurement delays due to PDU staff’s lack of experience and heavy workload. | Organizational | “PDU staff have no experience in using World Bank Procurement Regulations and have a heavy workload.” |
| R12 | Delays in preparing specifications and Terms of Reference. | Organizational | “Delays in preparing specifications, statement of requirements, and ToRs by the User Departments.” |
| R13 | Vendor payments delayed by internal approval bottlenecks. | Organizational | “Delays in paying vendors due to delays in internal approving processes.” |
| R14 | Staff turnover reduces institutional memory and continuity. | Organizational | “Turnover of qualified and experienced staff is noticed.” |
| R15 | Large refugee influx increases pressure on water resources and host communities. | External | “An estimated one million South Sudanese refugees have already migrated to Uganda… pressure on Uganda’s public services and natural resources.” |
| R16 | Long water‑collection distances increase gender‑based violence (GBV) risk. | Stakeholder | “Women and girls bear the heaviest burden for water collection. Long walks… trigger serious social consequences, including GBV.” |
| R17 | Labor influx may lead to GBV and other social issues. | Stakeholder | “Measures to address labour influx include a code of conduct… to minimize any potential GBV in the Project areas.” |
| R18 | Coordination among many agencies may cause implementation delays. | Stakeholder / Organizational | “Given the number of departments… the WESLD will take responsibility for overall coordination and communication.” |
| R19 | Regional instability from the South‑Sudan conflict threatens project execution. | Political / External | “The most critical risk to this outlook is regional instability, particularly from the ongoing conflict in South Sudan.” |
| R20 | Climate‑change‑induced floods and droughts threaten water supply reliability. | Environmental / External | “A high‑level screening… extreme temperature… increase in precipitation… likely to cause floods.” |

**Step 3 – Evidence filter**  
All listed risks are directly supported by quoted statements; none are removed.

**Step 4 – Assessment (likelihood 1‑5, impact 1‑5) and mitigation**  

| ID | Likelihood | Impact | Justification (one‑line) | Mitigation (concrete) |
|----|------------|--------|--------------------------|-----------------------|
| R01 | 3 | 4 | Geotechnical gaps are recognised but can be addressed early. | Conduct comprehensive geotechnical investigations before final design; include contingency in budgets. |
| R02 | 3 | 4 | Dry‑season flow deficits are possible given climate variability. | Install flow‑monitoring devices; design intakes with buffer storage; enforce minimum‑EF compliance. |
| R03 | 3 | 3 | Leakage risk is moderate; regular O&M can control it. | Implement strict O&M protocols, periodic inspections, and rapid repair mechanisms. |
| R04 | 2 | 3 | AC pipe handling is planned with safeguards, lowering probability. | Follow ESMF asbestos‑handling procedures; use certified disposal contractors. |
| R05 | 2 | 4 | Small‑dam failure would be severe but design standards are in place. | Use qualified engineers, adhere to Small‑Dam Guidelines, conduct independent safety audits. |
| R06 | 3 | 3 | Expertise gap is noted; training can reduce it. | Provide targeted technical assistance and capacity‑building workshops for solar‑pump installation. |
| R07 | 3 | 4 | Cost under‑estimation has been observed in similar projects. | Use detailed cost estimates, apply a cost‑contingency buffer, and monitor expenditures monthly. |
| R08 | 3 | 4 | Some regions currently lack full cost recovery. | Review and adjust tariffs, improve billing systems, and strengthen revenue‑collection mechanisms. |
| R09 | 2 | 3 | Debt service is a small share of revenue but could affect cash flow. | Phase loan repayments, maintain cost‑recovery ratios above 1.1, explore refinancing options. |
| R10 | 3 | 3 | UWAs’ capital needs exceed current donor support. | Establish a revolving financing facility and progressive tariff policy to build internal funding. |
| R11 | 4 | 3 | PDU inexperience is highlighted; likely to cause delays. | Recruit a procurement consultant experienced with World Bank rules; provide on‑the‑job training. |
| R12 | 3 | 3 | Specification delays have been noted in past work. | Assign dedicated technical officers to draft ToRs early; set firm internal deadlines. |
| R13 | 3 | 3 | Internal approval bottlenecks are documented. | Implement a payment‑tracking system with clear SLA for approvals; senior management oversight. |
| R14 | 3 | 2 | Staff turnover is moderate; impacts knowledge continuity. | Offer retention incentives, document procedures, and ensure hand‑over plans. |
| R15 | 4 | 4 | Refugee arrivals are ongoing and large. | Coordinate with UNHCR for joint water‑service planning; scale up infrastructure and allocate buffer water supplies. |
| R16 | 3 | 4 | GBV linked to water collection is a serious social impact. | Locate water points within 200 m of households; conduct gender‑sensitive community awareness campaigns. |
| R17 | 3 | 3 | Labour influx can exacerbate GBV if unmanaged. | Include a Labour‑Influx Management Plan and enforce contractor code‑of‑conduct; monitor compliance. |
| R18 | 3 | 3 | Multi‑agency coordination is complex. | Strengthen the PST, schedule regular inter‑agency coordination meetings, and use a shared project management platform. |
| R19 | 3 | 4 | Conflict spill‑over risk is moderate but high impact. | Maintain security monitoring, develop contingency scenarios, and keep flexible implementation schedules. |
| R20 | 4 | 4 | Climate extremes are increasingly likely and highly disruptive. | Integrate climate‑resilient designs (e.g., flood‑proof structures, water‑storage), implement catchment protection, and use early‑warning systems. |

**Step 5 – Consolidation**  
All 20 risks are distinct and supported by the appraisal document. No duplicates remain.
